sections.name: Store Home (Home Tab)

items.label: The Problem
items.text: The workspace tells a rep where things are, never what to do. Five tabs each hold their own queue, and every one of them is a pull: the rep has to open Orders to discover four orders are sitting unsubmitted, open My Team(s) to discover three Roster Bank captures are uncommitted, open Products to discover a bundle went Incomplete, and open Settings to discover the ship-to address they cleared is blocking freight. Nothing surfaces the union of those queues, so the cost of missing one is paid by a parent who cannot order or a container that misses MOQ.

items: The Store Setup Guide was written for a different problem and deliberately does not solve this one. It is orientation — explanatory, one-time, dismissible, and explicitly not a checklist or a progress tracker (Tabbed Store Dashboard, Epic B). A rep on their twentieth store, mid-window, with a live storefront, has no orientation problem and a substantial operational one.

There is also no continuity between sessions. A rep who is mid-way through re-pricing a category, or halfway through committing Roster Bank captures, closes the tab and comes back to the workspace root. The work is saved; the place is not. On a League store with divisions, teams, and a large catalog, re-finding the thing you were editing is a real tax.

items.label: What testing found
items.text: Usability testing produced four findings that this page exists to answer. They are quoted rather than paraphrased because the phrasing is the finding.

items.label: The workspace already has a landing surface, and it is empty
items.text: "I literally keep coming here and I'm like, where's everything I've been working on? Because this is the place it keeps going back to." The tester is describing a place the product returns them to repeatedly that holds no record of their work. This is not a request for a new destination — it is a report that the existing one is doing nothing.

items.label: There is no instruction at the point of return
items.text: "It's very like — there's not even instruction here."

items.label: My Team(s) is the highest-friction tab by a distance
items.text: "I don't know if you guys notice how often I got stuck on my teams. Like that was the biggest piece for me."

items.label: The core problem statement, verbatim
items.text: "I don't know what to do. I don't know where to go from here. There needs to be more guidance."

items: The last quote contains two distinct asks and they map onto the two working sections of this page: "I don't know what to do" is answered by Needs your attention, and "I don't know where to go from here" is answered by Pick up where you left off and by every deep link on the page.

The critical reading is that "there needs to be more guidance" is not a request for instructional content. The tester who said it had unresolved work in the store — they could not see it. The answer is to surface state they already own, not to write more explanation.

items.label: The Solution
items.text: A Home tab, first in the workspace navigation, with two working sections and a summary rail.

items: Needs your attention is a prioritized, finite list of resolvable conditions — each one an existing state defined by an existing spec, each one carrying a single action that deep-links to the surface that owns it. It is a derived read layer: it computes nothing, stores nothing, and enforces nothing. Every condition it can show is enumerated in Epic C, and a condition may not appear on Home unless it is defined by a published MVP spec.

Pick up where you left off is a per-rep, per-store list of the rep's own recent authoring actions, each with a deep link back to the surface where it happened. It reports location, not completion — the same honesty constraint the Setup Guide's progress bar carries.
In your store is a summary rail of counts and their attention overlays, giving the rep the shape of the store at a glance and a second route into each tab.

Three further panels answer "where's everything" for the things reps look for most: a Team Managers list they can add to, a brand assets panel holding the team logo and colors, and — on League stores — a structure directory of divisions and teams that routes into My Team(s).
Home is never a gate. It blocks nothing, requires no acknowledgement, and no store action depends on having visited it.
Who is this for? The store owner (rep) operating a single store, in any lifecycle state.

items.label: OPEN — to be confirmed, and it is not a question about whether the Home tab is conditional
items.text: whether the Team Manager Portal gains an equivalent surface. That portal is not the store workspace and does not render the six-tab navigation at all — it is specified as exactly two areas, Reporting and Rosters, scoped to one store (Store General Settings, Epic A2b). So the question is "does the portal get a third area", which is a separate scope decision, not a rule about this tab. Recommendation: no, this version. Almost every Epic C condition resolves to a surface a manager cannot reach, so a manager-facing equivalent would list actions they are not permitted to take. Confirm before build.

items.label: Scenarios encountered
items.text: Landing back on the workspace for the fourth time in a session and needing to see the work already in progress; opening a store and not knowing which of five tabs the next action lives behind; returning to a League store and needing to get back to the one division of eleven that was mid-edit; getting lost inside My Team(s) between the canvas, a division, a team, its roster, and the Roster Bank, and needing a route back to the last place that mattered; being an experienced rep for whom the Setup Guide will never auto-present again and having no other in-product orientation; opening a store mid-window and needing to know what is waiting; returning to a store after a week away; discovering that pending orders cannot be submitted because a division has no manager assigned; finding out that a bundle dropped off the storefront when its second item was removed; noticing that six rostered players still have not ordered required gear with the window closing; realizing a decorated product never became visible because its renders were still processing; picking back up a half-finished re-pricing pass on the Fan Gear category; coming back to a League store and resuming the division whose teams were being assigned products; entering a Draft store and being told the one thing standing between it and launch; entering a closed store and being routed to the Close Report; opening an Archived store and seeing a read-only summary with no actions offered.

blocks.heading: User Stories
items: Stories marked [UT] come directly from the testing findings above and should not be cut without revisiting them.
[UT] As a rep returning to the workspace, I want the place the product keeps landing me on to show me what I have been working on, so that arriving somewhere is not the same as arriving nowhere.
[UT] As a rep, I want to know what to do next without asking anyone, so that "I don't know where to go from here" is not how a session starts.
[UT] As a rep, I want that answer to be about my actual store rather than a generic setup lecture, so that guidance is worth reading on my twentieth store as well as my first.
[UT] As a rep working in My Team(s), I want to get back to the division, team, or roster I was in, so that a deep structure is not re-navigated from the top on every visit.
[UT] As a rep who has been oriented once already, I want help that is still there on my fifth store of the same type, so that the one-time guide having already fired does not leave me with nothing.
As a rep, I want one place that tells me what is waiting on me across all five tabs, so that I am not opening each one to find out.
As a rep, I want the thing that is actually blocking buyers ranked above the thing that is merely untidy, so that I fix the expensive problem first.
As a rep, I want each item to take me straight to where I fix it, so that reading about a problem and solving it are one motion rather than two.
As a rep, I want the list to be honest about being finite — if there are only two things, I want to see two things, not two things and eight suggestions.
As a rep, I want an empty list to say so plainly, so that "nothing needs me" is information rather than an absence.
As a rep, I want to be returned to the work I was doing last session, so that continuity is not something I reconstruct by hand.
As a rep, I want that trail to be mine, so that another rep's edits on a shared store are not presented to me as my own unfinished work.
As a rep on a Draft store, I want to know the single thing standing between me and launch, so that pre-launch is one clear step rather than a scavenger hunt.
As a rep, I want the counts on Home to match the counts on the tabs exactly, so that I trust Home enough to stop checking behind it.
As an experienced rep, I want Home to stay out of my way when there is nothing to do, so that a hub does not become a chore.

requirements.subtitle: Epic A — The Home tab & workspace navigation
requirements.link: Technical Spec: Store Home (Home Tab) — Epic A — The Home tab & workspace navigation

blocks.heading: Epic A — The Home tab & workspace navigation

items.label: Sixth tab, first position
items.text: Given a rep opens a store workspace, when the navigation renders, then it presents six tabs in order: Home, My Team(s), Products, Orders, Reports, Settings. Home is first.

items.label: Home is a permanent tab, on exactly the same footing as the other five
items.text: It is always present in the navigation, in every store state (Draft, Open, Closed, Archived), on both store types (Individual Team, League), and on both distribution formats (pop-up, always-on). It is never hidden, never disabled, never conditional, and never removed — there is no store configuration in which the workspace has five tabs. A rep who learns Home is there learns it once.

items.label: What varies is the content inside two of its sections, not the tab
items.text: The precedent is the Settings tab: it carries seven sections, one of which (Catalog & Decoration) renders only when a third-party vendor is enabled — and the Settings tab is permanent regardless. Home has the same shape. Every store-state and store-type rule in Epic C governs which cards populate one section, exactly as the vendor flag governs one Settings section. None of it reaches the tab.

items.label: The tab's structure is stable too
items.text: The summary rail (Epic E) always renders, including at zero. The attention section (Epic C) always renders, including when it has nothing to report. Only the resume trail (Epic D) can be absent, and only because an empty trail carries no information at all.

items.label: The five existing tabs are unchanged
items.text: Home composes their state; it takes nothing from them and moves nothing into itself. Every tab's contents remain owned by its own spec.

items.label: Tab count is no longer fixed at five
items.text: The Tabbed Store Dashboard shell must be amended — see Appendix A. The shell owns the tab set; it does not own Home's contents, exactly as it does not own the Settings tab's section list.

items.label: Attention badges on tab labels
items.text: Given one or more Epic C conditions resolve to a given tab, when the navigation renders, then that tab label carries a dot indicator. The dot reflects presence, not count — the count lives in the summary rail and in the attention list, and a number in the nav would be a third place for the same figure to drift.

items.label: Blocking-tier conditions produce the dot; Informational-tier conditions do not
items.text: An always-on informational item would leave a permanent dot on Settings and train reps to ignore it.

items.label: Home is the default landing tab on workspace entry
items.text: Given a rep opens a store workspace, when no deep link specifies a tab, then Home is shown.

items.label: The reasoning, stated precisely
items.text: The place the tester kept returning to was the My Team(s) tab — they were using a working tab as a de facto hub, and it does not hold a record of their work because that is not what it is for. The decision taken was to build a surface for that job rather than load more of it onto My Team(s). Home is therefore the default because the alternative is reps continuing to treat some other tab as the hub, which is the behaviour that produced the finding.

items.label: The quote alone does not carry this
items.text: "This is the place it keeps going back to" describes My Team(s), not an empty landing page, so it is evidence that reps want a hub — not evidence about which tab should open first. The default-landing decision rests on the design choice above, and should be revisited against the sessions where Home is the only tab visited metric rather than treated as research-backed.

items.label: No per-rep or per-store override in v1
items.text: A configurable landing tab was considered and cut: it adds a preference, a settings surface to hold it, and a second entry path to reason about, in exchange for saving one click for reps who would rather start on Orders. Revisit against the sessions where Home is the only tab visited metric — if Home is routinely bounced through, the preference is worth building.

items.label: Deep links always win
items.text: A link into Orders, a Settings section key, or a My Team(s) division jump-in opens its target directly. Home is the default, not an interstitial.

items.label: Scope is confirmed as store-level
items.text: The tester meant the My Team(s) tab, which sits inside the store workspace — not the Team Stores Landing Page or the Stores directory. So the problem is at store level and this page addresses the right instance of it. A workspace-level equivalent remains out of scope.

items.label: Home does not replace the workspace header
items.text: The store status chip, the storefront URL, the Preview Store control, and the Setup Guide re-entry point remain in the header where they are specified (Launch & Status Controls; Tabbed Store Dashboard, Epic B). Home may echo header state in its summary strip but is not the authoring surface for any of it.

requirements.subtitle: Epic B — Interaction with the two existing auto-presenting sequences
requirements.link: Technical Spec: Store Home (Home Tab) — Epic B — Interaction with the two existing auto-presenting sequences

blocks.heading: Epic B — Interaction with the two existing auto-presenting sequences
items: Two paced card sequences already trigger on "first workspace entry": the Store Setup Guide (first entry after store creation) and the Store Close Report (first entry after a close event) — see System Modals & Toasts. Home now sits behind both of them, so their ordering has to be stated.

items.label: Both sequences take precedence over Home
items.text: Given either sequence's trigger condition is met, when the rep enters the workspace, then the sequence presents over Home. Home renders beneath and is fully available on dismissal.

items.label: They never both fire
items.text: A store cannot be simultaneously newly-created-and-unlaunched and freshly-closed. No ordering rule between the two is required, and none should be built.

items.label: Home does not re-arm, re-trigger, or replace either sequence
items.text: The Setup Guide's seen-state remains per rep per store type; the Close Report's remains per user per close event. Home reads neither flag and writes neither.

items.label: Home carries the Setup Guide's re-entry point as a secondary affordance
items.text: Given any store in any state, when Home renders, then a reopen-the-setup-guide link is present. This is a second entry point to the existing header control, not a new one — opening from Home behaves identically to opening from the header (lands on card 1, no forced pacing, regardless of seen-state).

items.label: The Close Report entry point is likewise echoed, not owned
items.text: Given a Closed or Archived store, then Home surfaces a route to the Close Report. Availability, disabled-state copy, and review-mode behavior are owned by Store Status & Lifecycle, Epic H.

requirements.subtitle: Epic C — Needs your attention: the attention-card catalogue
requirements.link: Technical Spec: Store Home (Home Tab) — Epic C — Needs your attention: the attention-card catalogue

blocks.heading: Epic C — Needs your attention: the attention-card catalogue (High-impact)
items: Scope of this Epic, stated first because the word "condition" invites a misreading. A condition here is a store state that causes a card to appear inside the Needs your attention section. It is a row-level rule about card population. Nothing in this Epic governs whether the Home tab exists, renders, or appears in the navigation — Home is permanent and unconditional (Epic A). Read every rule below as "which cards are in the list", never as "whether the tab is there".
Concretely:

items.label: The tab always renders
items.text: Six tabs, every store, every state.

items.label: The section always renders
items.text: Given zero conditions hold, the section is present and says so — an empty list is a first-class state (Governing rule 3), not a hidden section.

items.label: The cards vary
items.text: A Draft store and a closed League store surface different cards because they are in different states, the same way the Orders tab shows different rows to different stores without the Orders tab becoming conditional.

items: This Epic is the substance of the feature. Every card Home can surface is registered here with its owning spec, tier, trigger, and resolution route. A condition not in this table produces no card.

Reading the table. Trigger is the state that makes the card appear — expressed against the owning spec's own state, never against a figure Home computes. Resolves to is the deep-link target. Clears when is the state change that removes the card; there is no manual dismissal (see below).

The Condition column is an internal name. It is not card copy, and must never be shipped as card copy. Rep-facing headlines and detail lines are specified separately in Epic I. This distinction matters because it has already cost a design round: a prototype rendered "Freight routing unresolved — 2 pending containers can't be submitted" straight from the C-03 row, which describes an internal routing state rather than the action the rep needs to take — a direct violation of the rule two sections up (a Blocking condition always names who is blocked) and of Epic I's name the consequence, not the internal state. Internal names are for engineers reading the catalogue. Card copy is in Epic I and nowhere else.

blocks.heading: C1 — Orders
items: ID · Condition · Tier · Trigger (owning spec) · Resolves to · Clears when

items.label: Condition
items.text: Pending orders awaiting submission

items.label: Tier
items.text: Action

items.label: Trigger (owning spec)
items.text: ≥1 order in the storefront → pending state, not yet submitted to the factory (Order Management, Epic A)

items.label: Resolves to

items.label: Clears when

items.label: Condition

items.label: Tier
items.text: Informational

items.label: Trigger (owning spec)
items.text: ≥1 pending group below its minimum-quantity threshold (Order Management, Epic B)

items.label: Resolves to
items.text: Orders → Pending Orders, scrolled to that group

items.label: Clears when
items.text: Group reaches MOQ, or is submitted short

items.label: Condition
items.text: Manager unassigned on a division or team with pending orders

items.label: Tier
items.text: Blocking

items.label: Trigger (owning spec)
items.text: ≥1 pending group whose group or team manager is unassigned (Order Management, Epic B; Store General Settings, Epic A3)

items.label: Resolves to
items.text: Settings → Distribution & Fulfillment, with the affected division auto-opened

items.label: Clears when
items.text: Every assigned group has a resolved manager

items.label: Condition
items.text: No ship-to destination address

items.label: Tier
items.text: Blocking

items.label: Trigger (owning spec)
items.text: Fulfillment method is Ship to Team Manager and the destination address is empty (Store General Settings, Epic A3)

items.label: Resolves to
items.text: Settings → Distribution & Fulfillment → Fulfillment Method

items.label: Clears when
items.text: A verified destination address exists

items.label: Condition
items.text: Rostered players missing required gear

items.label: Tier
items.text: Action

items.label: Trigger (owning spec)
items.text: ≥1 committed player record with un-ordered Team Required gear (Order Management, Epic C; Roster Management, Epic 2)

items.label: Resolves to
items.text: My Team(s) → store-wide player view, filtered to incomplete

items.label: Clears when
items.text: Every rostered player's required gear is ordered or opted out

items.label: C-01 uses the owning spec's verb
items.text: The Orders tab's action is Submit — Submit Group, Submit Selected, Submit All — and the state is Pending. Home says "n pending orders to submit", not "approve n orders". There is no approval step in the product: pending orders are submitted to the factory in batches, deliberately held to hit MOQ, and "approve" would imply a review gate that does not exist while obscuring the MOQ workflow the Pending sub-tab exists for.

items.label: C-03 and C-04 are separate conditions with one consequence
items.text: Both block pending-order submission, and a store can hold both at once. They are not merged, because they resolve to different controls and a merged card would send the rep to the wrong one.

items.label: When C-03 suppresses C-08, C-03's copy must carry C-08's substance
items.text: C-03 is the same underlying problem as C-08 with orders now waiting on it, and the suppression rule below means only C-03 renders for an affected division. So C-03 must name the specific divisions or teams — "Division 3 and Division 7" — not just a count. The prototype did this correctly and it should be treated as required, not incidental: without the names, the rep lands in Distribution & Fulfillment with no idea which rows to fix.

items.label: C-05 respects the opt-out flag
items.text: A product with Allow opt-out enabled counts a player's "I already own this" as satisfied (Products Tab, Epic E), and a player who has opted out is not counted as missing.

items.label: C-05 does not offer Send Reminder from Home
items.text: Reminders are per player, are disabled for players with no contact channel, and are sent from the player drawer (Roster Management, Epic 2). Home routes; it does not send.

items.text: Capture counts are already specified to surface on team cards, division cards, and the stats header (Roster Management, Epic 5) — Home is a fourth read of the same count, not a new one.

items.label: C-07 mirrors the amber gap state, and must use the same language
items.text: The canvas already renders a team with no products as amber "No products yet" rather than blank. Home's card is the store-level roll-up of that same condition.

items.label: C-08 is the unassigned precursor to C-03
items.text: C-08 is Action tier because nothing is blocked yet; C-03 is Blocking because an order is now waiting on it. Both may be present. Where both are present for the same division, C-03 suppresses C-08 for that division — the blocking card already routes to the same control, and showing both would double-count one problem.

blocks.heading: On the My Team(s) finding — three conditions is probably the right number, and attention cards are probably not the fix.
items: Testing named My Team(s) as "the biggest piece" of the friction, but only three registered conditions resolve to it, and that is not an oversight to correct. My Team(s) is the most structurally complex surface in the product — divisions, standalone teams, rosters, player records, the Roster Bank, per-roster duplicate-number policy, fulfillment mapping, and League product coverage, across seven Epics — and almost none of that complexity produces a resolvable condition. It produces a navigation problem. The tester said they got stuck, not that they missed something.
That points the fix at Epic D and at deep-link scoping, not at more cards:

items.label: The resume trail matters more here than anywhere else
items.text: A rep returning to "division 7 → U12 Blue → roster" is four levels deep. Every other tab's deepest resumable target is a product detail page. The resume trail's value is concentrated in this tab, and the trail's row count and expiry should be tuned for the My Team(s) case rather than the Products case.

items.label: My Team(s) deep links must land scoped, not at the canvas
items.text: C-06's store-wide Roster Bank view, C-07's division coverage table, and every resume row targeting a team must open at that entity with breadcrumbs intact — the existing jump-in pattern that auto-opens a targeted division. A card that dumps the rep on the canvas to find the team themselves reproduces the problem it was meant to solve.

items.label: "Got stuck" meant lost, not confused — confirmed
items.text: The tester could not find or return to a place; they were not struggling to understand divisions vs. teams vs. rosters. That settles where the fix belongs: Epic D and deep-link scoping, not orientation content. It also means the Setup Guide's league card set is not implicated, and Home is not being asked to explain the structure — only to get the rep back into it. Every My Team(s) route on this page is therefore load-bearing rather than convenient.

blocks.heading: On adding rosters to the attention list — where this landed.
items: "Add roster(s) to Needs your attention" had three candidate meanings. After prototype review, only one card remains.
Reading · Status · Why

items.label: Rosters with uncommitted Roster Bank captures
Status
items.text: Registered as C-06

items.label: Why
items.text: Real queued work, finite, and it clears

items.label: Rosters with players who can't be reached
Status
items.text: Not a card — carried on C-05's detail line

items.label: Why
items.text: Would be permanently present; see below

items.label: Teams that have no roster yet
Status
items.text: Not registered — recommend against

items.label: Why
items.text: Reverses a decided direction; see below

items: Why the uncontactable-players card was withdrawn, and the general rule it establishes. It would have flagged committed player records carrying neither an email nor a phone. Prototype review established that reps and team managers commonly hold contact details for only a minority of their players — so the condition would hold on nearly every store, nearly always. A condition that is true in the common case is not an attention condition; it is a permanent fixture, and a permanent card trains reps to skip the list. That is the same reasoning behind Informational conditions not producing navigation dots, and behind Governing rule 3's insistence that an empty list is the success state.

The underlying problem is real and is handled at the point of use instead. A rep acting on C-05 lands in the player drawer and finds Send Reminder disabled and Share Team Store Link reduced to copy-only for players with no contact channel. So C-05's detail line carries the caveat — "n of them have no email or phone, so a reminder won't reach them" — which puts the warning exactly where the rep is about to need it rather than on a card they will learn to ignore. C-15 inherits the same caveat, since its remedy is also reminders.

items.label: This is a finding about the roster feature set, not only about Home
items.text: If most players have no contact channel, then Send Reminder and the share-link flow are less useful in practice than Roster Management assumes, and the metric that tab already tracks — share of committed records carrying a contact channel — is the one to look at. Worth raising with whoever owns that spec; it is out of scope here.

items.label: C-25's ID is retired, not reused
items.text: A future roster condition takes the next free number, so that a reference to C-25 in a ticket or a design file never resolves to something different from what it meant.

items: Why "teams with no roster" is the one to be careful about. Rosters are optional, are never a launch prerequisite, and a team may exist with no roster at all. That is not an oversight — it is the finding the roster-optional work was built on: research with high-value reps found requiring a roster up front unacceptable, and the spec's framing is that reps "do not reject player tracking; they reject the roster as an upfront obligation. The roster's outputs are valuable; the roster as a gate is not." A card headed "3 teams have no roster" reintroduces the obligation through the back door — a gate in everything but enforcement, on the highest-traffic surface in the workspace. It would also fail the same always-on test C-25 just failed.
Unchanged: a roster that is merely incomplete is not a condition. There is no known true team size to compare against, so "incomplete" is unmeasurable as well as undesirable.

items.text: A render-pending item is in a normal transient state that resolves itself; a failed render never resolves without the rep, and the item can never become visible until it does.

items: C-12 is Blocking because a bundle in this state has already dropped off the storefront and cannot satisfy the launch gate. This is the tail of the two-member-removal modal (System Modals & Toasts) — the modal warns at the moment of removal, Home is what catches the rep who clicked through it.

items.label: There is no "size run" concept, and C-13 is not a purchase blocker
items.text: Products carry size bands (Youth / Adult) with base costs, and separately an application sizing confirmation state per decoration row. Neither gates launch and neither stops a buyer ordering a visible product. So C-13's copy must never claim "customers can't order these yet" — the genuine can't-order conditions are C-10 and C-11. If a real size-run gate is ever wanted, that is a change to the Products spec, not a Home card.

items.label: Conditions enforced at save do not appear here
items.text: Uncategorized products and League TR/TS items with zero team assignment are both blocked at every save surface (Products Tab, Governing rule 2 and Epic L), so neither can exist to be surfaced. Adding a card for a state the system already prevents would imply the enforcement is unreliable.

items.label: C-27 is Action, not Blocking, and the distinction matters
items.text: An orphaned product stays visible and purchasable — nothing is unpublished, no cart is affected, no order is touched. What it loses is its place in the storefront’s category filtering and search, and its grouping in category-based reporting. Buyers are not stopped, so Blocking would overstate it; rep work is queued and degrades the store while it waits, which is Action.

items.label: C-27 originates outside the store, which is why it needs a card at all
items.text: Every other condition in this catalogue is produced by something happening inside the store the rep is looking at. This one is produced by a workspace-level deletion that may have been performed by a different rep, on a different day, affecting several stores at once. Nothing in the store’s own workflow would surface it.

items.label: C-27 clears only by re-filing
items.text: Recreating a category with the same name does not reattach orphaned products, because a recreated category is a new record.

items.label: C-14 and C-15 are deliberately two cards, not one
items.text: It is tempting to merge "store closes in 18 days" with "6 players haven't ordered" into a single urgent card. They are two conditions with two different triggers and two different resolutions; merged, the card carries two verbs and the rep has to pick. C-14 is the clock. C-15 is the clock plus a consequence, and only C-15 is worth an Action-tier prompt.

items.text: The Active Order Window card's days-left pill already turns urgent inside the final 7 days (Store General Settings, Epic E). Home reads that same resolved state. C-14 matches the pill at 7 days. C-15 fires earlier, at 14 days, because the action it asks for — chasing parents who have not ordered — takes days to land, and a buyer-facing countdown is not built to give the rep lead time.

items.label: "Extend deadline" is not a Home action, because no such control exists
items.text: Extending a window is an edit to the store schedule in Settings; on a store that has already auto-closed it additionally requires a Re-open (Store Status & Lifecycle, Epic D). Home routes to Edit Store Schedule and uses that name. A one-click extend would be a new control in the Settings spec, not something Home can offer.

items.label: C-18 and C-20 mirror the Close Report's needs-attention strip
items.text: Both are already specified as detail-layer callouts on the Close Report. Home surfaces them for the rep who is back in the workspace weeks after dismissing it.

items.text: The spec states plainly that disabled-with-exemptions is expected, not a defect. Home reports it and offers a route; it must not imply the rep did something wrong.

items.label: A condition must be false on a well-run store
items.text: Before registering anything, check whether it would hold in the common case. If it would, it is a permanent fixture rather than an attention condition, and a permanent card teaches reps to skip the list. The uncontactable-players condition was withdrawn on exactly this test. Where the underlying warning still matters, attach it to the detail line of a card the rep will act on, or to the surface where they will hit it.

items.label: Ordering
items.text: Blocking → Action → Informational. Within a tier, order by cost of delay, defined as a fixed per-condition rank recorded in the catalogue above, not by recency and not by count. A rep should see the same order twice in a row for the same store state.

items.label: Cap the list at five
items.text: Decided; tune against the cards-rendered distribution metric. Given more than five conditions resolve, when the section renders, then the top five are shown by the ordering above with a "n more" expander. A hub that renders fourteen cards is a backlog, and a backlog is the thing reps already have.

items.label: Blocking-tier conditions are never collapsed into the expander
items.text: If more than five Blocking conditions hold, all of them render and the cap is exceeded. This is the one case where the cap yields.

items.text: Given four orders are pending, then one C-01 card renders naming the count — not four cards. Per-record detail belongs to the owning tab.

items.label: Cards state the count and the oldest age where age is meaningful
items.text: "Oldest placed 3 days ago" is required on C-01, C-05, and C-06 — the three conditions where the passage of time has an operational cost.

items.label: No manual dismissal
items.text: A condition clears when its underlying state clears, per the Clears when column. Nothing on Home can be snoozed, hidden, or marked done, because Home holds no state (Governing rule 1) and a dismissible card would need somewhere to remember the dismissal. Where a rep legitimately wants to accept a condition rather than fix it, the acceptance is expressed in the owning surface — closing a coverage gap, submitting short, deleting the bundle.

items.label: Empty state is a first-class state
items.text: Given zero conditions resolve, when the section renders, then it states plainly that nothing needs the rep right now and names the store's current lifecycle state. It does not manufacture suggestions, and it does not surface Informational-tier filler to avoid looking empty.

items.label: Every card carries exactly one primary action
items.text: Where a condition has two plausible resolutions, it is two conditions (see C-03/C-04) or the card routes to the surface where both are available.

requirements.name: Functional Requirements & Core Workflows
requirements.subtitle: Epic D — Recently worked on
requirements.link: Technical Spec: Store Home (Home Tab) — Epic D — Recently worked on

blocks.heading: Epic D — Recently worked on (High-impact)
items: The second question in the brief: how does the system know where you left off? It does not, today — nothing persists it. This Epic specifies what would have to exist, and is deliberate about what the feature is and is not.

blocks.heading: What it is
items: A trail of the rep's own recent authoring actions in this store, each with a route back to where it happened. It is a location aid. It is not a task list, not a draft-recovery mechanism, and not a progress tracker.

items.label: This distinction is the whole design, and testing confirms it
items.text: The tester asked "where's everything I've been working on?" — an inventory question about work already done, not a request to finish something abandoned. Every candidate row points the same way: edited pricing, added 4 players, updated the banner image are all completed actions. Labeling them Resume implies the rep left something half-done, which is untrue and mildly accusatory. The section returns the rep to a place, and its copy must say so.

items.label: The section is named "Recently worked on", not "Pick up where you left off"
items.text: The original heading described resumption; the research describes recall. The rows contain completed work, and the heading now says so.

items.label: The precedent is already set in the product
items.text: The Setup Guide's progress bar indicates position in the sequence, not completion, and the owning spec forbids styling or labelling it as a completion indicator. The same rule applies here: this section shows where the rep was, and must never be styled or labelled as a to-do list, a completion percentage, or a readiness score.

items.label: A resume event is written on a rep-authored write
items.text: Given a rep performs a qualifying write against this store, when the write commits, then a resume event is recorded carrying: the acting rep, the store, the surface key (the deep-link target), an entity reference where one exists, a short human-readable label, and a timestamp.

items.label: The surface key is the same deep-link key the rest of the workspace already uses
items.text: Settings deep links resolve through a section key; My Team(s) jump-ins target a division; the Products catalog return path scrolls to and focuses a specific item. Resume reuses those routes. It must not introduce a parallel routing scheme.

items.label: The label is composed from the entity, not stored as prose
items.text: "Home Jersey — pricing" is rendered from a product reference plus a field group at read time, so a product renamed after the event resumes under its current name. A frozen label would show the rep a name that no longer exists in their catalog.

blocks.heading: What qualifies
items: Qualifies · Does not qualify

items.label: A write the rep authored
items.text: Any read, filter, sort, search, or tab switch

items.label: A write against a resumable surface — one with a stable deep link
items.text: A write with no addressable destination

items.label: A write against this store
items.text: Writes in other stores, or at workspace scope

items.label: The rep's own writes
items.text: Another rep's, a team manager's, a buyer's, or the system's

items.label: Buyer and system writes never qualify
items.text: An order placed by a parent, a checkout address written back onto a roster, a Roster Bank capture created by a storefront order, an auto-close, a render completing — none of these are the rep's work and none belong in the rep's trail. Several of them are already surfaced properly as Epic C conditions, which is where a rep should meet them.

items.label: Bulk actions record one event, not n
items.text: A CSV import of forty players is one event ("imported 40 players"), and a bulk-pricing apply across a catalog is one event. The event references the operation, not each row.

items.label: Destructive actions do not qualify
items.text: Deleting a product, clearing a roster, or deleting a bundle produces no resume event. There is nothing to return to, and offering to "resume" a deletion is at best confusing.

items.label: Collapse by surface + entity, keeping the most recent
items.text: Given a rep edits one product's pricing four times in ten minutes, then one event is shown, timestamped at the most recent write. Without this the trail is a keystroke log.

items.label: Five visible by default, most recent first, expandable to fifteen
items.text: Decided. A shorter list was considered, on the reasoning that a browsable trail becomes an audit log. The testing quote argues the other way: "where's everything I've been working on" is a request for coverage, not for the last thing touched, and a three-row list on a store where the rep has been working across teams, products, and settings in one session will not contain what they are looking for. The audit-log risk is real and is bounded by the ceiling, by expiry, and by collapsing on surface + entity — not by keeping the list too short to be useful.

items.label: Events expire after 30 days
items.text: Decided. A rep who steps away from a store for three weeks mid-season is the case that most needs the trail, and they are exactly who a two-week window locks out. The counter-argument is that a month-old edit is noise; that is what ordering by recency is for.

items.text: The deepest and most expensive re-navigation in the product is a League store's division → team → roster path, and the trail's parameters should be set so that path is reliably recoverable.

items.label: Per rep, always
items.text: Given two reps co-manage a store, then each sees only their own trail. A shared trail would present another rep's work as the reader's unfinished business — the failure mode the "whose work is this" rule exists to prevent.

items: Given the rep has no qualifying events, when the section renders, then it is absent, not empty. An empty resume list carries no information and occupies the space the attention list needs.

blocks.heading: Epic E — In your store (summary rail)
items: A per-tab summary giving the rep the shape of the store and a second route into each tab. Purely derived (Governing rule 1).

items.label: One row per tab, in navigation order
items.text: My Team(s), Products, Orders, Reports.

items.label: Each row's label matches its tab's label exactly — the first row reads My Team(s), not Rosters
items.text: Decided. The prototypes relabelled it Rosters / Roster while the navigation beside it still read My Teams / My Team; that is two names for one destination, which Governing rule 1 forbids, and the rail's whole purpose is being a second route into the tab.

items.label: The roster figures live in the sub-line
items.text: The row's content is roster-centric, which is what the rename was reaching for, and the sub-line delivers it without forking the label.

items: On a League store the label is also inaccurate, not just inconsistent: My Team(s) holds divisions, teams, rosters, product coverage, and fulfillment mapping. "Rosters" narrows it to one of those, and it collides with the League structure panel two cards below, which reports the same player count.

items.label: The tab is not being renamed
items.text: "My Team(s)" stands, so the row matches it.

items.label: Roster entries are players, everywhere on Home
items.text: Decided. The prototypes said 148 players on the League store and 18 members on the Individual Team store; "members" is dropped. Verify that Roster Management's own stats header says players too — if it says members, that spec and this one must be reconciled rather than diverging (Governing rule 1).

items.label: Each row carries the tab's headline count and, where one exists, its attention overlay
items.text: "148 players · 5 Roster Bank captures", "24 orders · 4 to submit". The overlay is the same figure the corresponding Epic C card names — not a second computation of it.

items.label: Counts come from the owning tab
items.text: Player counts exclude captures (Roster Management, Epic 5); catalog counts follow the catalog's own count; order counts follow the Orders tab's. Home must not define what counts as a member, a product, or an order.

items.label: No fundraising progress bar, because there is no goal to progress toward

items.label: What Home may show instead

items.label: Reports row is a route, not a KPI strip
items.text: The Reports tab and the workspace Overview own the store's analytics. Home does not restate revenue, dealer profit, or fundraising breakdowns — a third rendering of those figures is a third thing to drift.

items.label: Rows are always present, including at zero
items.text: "0 products" on a Draft store is the most useful thing that row can say.

requirements.name: Functional Requirements & Core Workflows
requirements.subtitle: Epic F — Team Managers panel
requirements.link: Technical Spec: Store Home (Home Tab) — Epic F — Team Managers panel

blocks.heading: Epic F — Team Managers panel
items: A list of this store's managers with the ability to add one, hosted on Home under the one value, two surfaces clause in Governing rule 1.

blocks.heading: What it is

items.label: The same collection, not a copy
items.text: The panel reads and writes the manager collection owned by Store General Settings, Epic A2c — the same collection written by Step 1 — Basics Epic E and by coach import from the Team Database. There is no Home-local manager record and no separate storage.

items.label: Read view
items.text: one row per manager showing Name, Email, Phone, and Contact Preference. The panel is titled League Manager Information on League stores and Team Manager Information on Individual Team stores, matching the Settings card.

items.label: The designated record is tagged "Point of Contact"
items.text: Adopting the exact name of the setting it feeds — Store General Settings, Epic A2's Store Point of Contact — rather than inventing a near-synonym. This is the strongest form of Governing rule 1's no-new-vocabulary clause: the tag is not a new term at all, it is a pointer to an existing one. Bare Primary is banned because it reads as a rank or a manager type, implying a status field the product does not have, and Primary Contact was a third term for something already named. The underlying designation is unchanged, and is not Home's to define. Epic A2c specifies it as an invariant — "exactly one record is designated primary at all times" — and four things depend on it: Epic A2's rule that Team Manager mode inherits from this record and that "non-primary manager records never feed the point of contact"; Epic A1's protection of it through a team re-bind; the Dependencies section's requirement for "a collection of manager records with exactly one designated primary"; and the tab's metric tracking changes to it. Only the rep-facing label moves. "Primary" remains fine as an internal field name, the way Epic C's condition names are internal.

items.label: Because the tag borrows the setting's name, it must render only when the setting actually resolves to that record
items.text: Point-of-contact mode is set per channel, and Email and Phone may each be Team Manager, Salesperson, or Custom (Epic A2). So:
items: Given at least one channel is on Team Manager mode, then the designated record is tagged Point of Contact.

Given both channels are on Salesperson or Custom, then no row is tagged, and the panel states at its foot who buyers actually see, with a route to the Store Point of Contact setting. Tagging a manager with the name of a setting that resolves to a salesperson would be a plain falsehood, and worse than the vague version because it borrows real authority.

Given only one channel is on Team Manager mode, then the row states which — "Point of Contact · email" — because the rep's coach supplies the published email while the phone belongs to someone else, and a bare tag would over-claim.

items.label: The tag renders on single-manager stores too
items.text: Suppressing it at one record would be right if the label were Primary — a rank with nothing to outrank is noise. Point of Contact carries different information: it tells the rep whose details parents see in the storefront footer, which is worth stating most on a store with one manager, since a rep with a single coach is the likeliest not to know that coach's email is published. Subject to the render rule above.

items.label: There is no role or title field, and that stays true
items.text: No "Coach", no "Team Mom" — and whether Team Database coach records even carry a role is an open dependency in Settings Epic A2c. "Point of Contact" is deliberately not that: it says which record buyers see, not what the person does for the team.

items.label: Settings must adopt the same term, and Home must not ship ahead of it
items.text: Settings currently marks the record primary. Two labels for one designation is the failure Governing rule 1 exists to prevent, and it would be Home that introduced it. See Appendix A, amendment 8e.

items: Invite is offered on every manager row carrying an email, per Settings Epic A2b. Given the person already holds an active or pending invite, then the row states that status in place of the action — "Portal access active" or "Invited, not signed in" — rather than silently omitting the button. An absent affordance reads as "not possible", not "already done", and the prototypes omitted it on managers who had emails on file with no explanation visible to the rep.

items.label: Add
items.text: an Add manager action opening the existing manager edit modal with its full field set (First Name, Last Name, Email, Phone Number, Street Address, Contact Preference) and its full validation. Not a reduced inline form — a truncated version would be a second implementation and would drop consequence disclosures.

items: Edit and remove are available on each row through the same modal, subject to every rule in Epic A2c: exactly one designated record at all times, removal of it blocked until another is designated, and any change to which record is designated stated before saving because it is buyer-visible. The invariants hold independently of the label — "Point of Contact" is presentation, and no display decision may become a data one.

blocks.heading: Designating the point of contact — Home displays it, Home does not set it
items: The designation is not set in the manager edit modal. It is set in Step 1 — Basics during store creation and in Settings → General. Confirmed on review, and it resolves what looked like a missing affordance: the manager modal was never the place, so Home opening the full shared modal correctly gives the rep no designation control.

items.label: Home shows the tag read-only and routes to Settings → General to change it
items.text: Given the rep wants to change which manager is the point of contact, then Home links them to Settings → General rather than hosting the change. This is the route rather than host branch of Governing rule 1: the control lives on a surface Home does not own, and the change is buyer-visible, so it happens where its full disclosure already lives.

items: Adding a manager never changes the designation, so Add manager needs no designation control of its own. Epic A1 is explicit that a connect "adds; it never replaces" and that no existing record is "overwritten, demoted, or deleted as a side effect." The first record on a new store becomes the point of contact by being the only one.

items.label: A rep must never be able to strand the designation from Home
items.text: Given a removal from Home would leave the collection without a designated record, then the removal is blocked with the reason stated and a route to Settings → General — the Epic A2c invariant, enforced from this surface as from any other.

blocks.heading: Adding a manager grants no access, and Home must say so in place
items: This is the sharpest risk in the whole request. The owning spec states the rule in absolute terms: a manager record "provisions no account, sends no email, and grants no portal access," and portal entitlement is created only by an explicit invite in Settings → People & Access. It calls this "the single most important constraint on the feature."
An Add manager button on the workspace's landing page is the most likely place in the product for a rep to assume they have just invited someone. So:

Given the manager modal is opened from Home, then it states that adding a manager creates a contact record only and does not grant portal access, and offers a route to Settings → People & Access to send an invite.

Given a manager row carries an email, then the panel offers Invite against it, routing to People & Access — so the rep is not retyping an address they just entered. This mirrors the affordance People & Access already offers against existing manager records.

Given a manager is removed from Home, then any invite issued to that person remains active until revoked in People & Access, and the confirmation says so and links there. Home may not infer, create, or revoke entitlement in either direction.

blocks.heading: Point-of-contact propagation
items: Given a point-of-contact channel is on Team Manager mode, when the primary manager's email or phone changes from Home, then the storefront footer reflects it with no further action — the existing live binding. The modal states this before saving, exactly as it does in Settings.

Home does not surface the Store Point of Contact mode selector. That lives in the Edit Store Details modal, and splitting a two-part setting across two surfaces is how one half gets edited without the other.

blocks.heading: Availability
items: The panel renders in every store state, because the manager collection is explicitly exempt from post-launch locking — coaching changes happen mid-season and must not require a store rebuild.
On Archived stores it renders read-only, with no add, edit, or remove.

Home's panel does not offer Add from Team Database. Settings' manager card does. Decided. Home carries Add manager only, and a rep who wants to pull an existing coach record is routed to Settings → General.

This is the route rather than host branch of Governing rule 1, and the same call as the point-of-contact designation above. Coach import is a selection flow over Team Database records — verification, multi-select, point-in-time copies — and it belongs on the surface that owns the manager collection rather than being reproduced on a landing page.
Settings Epic A1's standing open question closes as yes on the strength of this: the affordance goes on the manager card, which is where a rep looking to add a coach naturally goes (Appendix A, 8b).

items.label: Whichever surface adds the record, import grants no access
items.text: The no-portal-access rule covers the import path exactly as it covers a typed record; an imported coach is offered for Invite in People & Access the same way a hand-typed one is.

requirements.subtitle: Epic G — Brand assets panel
requirements.link: Technical Spec: Store Home (Home Tab) — Epic G — Brand assets panel

blocks.heading: Epic G — Brand assets panel
items: Team logo and team colors on Home, reusing the existing components.

blocks.heading: Three different things get called "logos and colors" — this panel surfaces two of them and links to the third
items: Asset · Scope · Owned by · On Home

items.label: Scope
items.text: Store-level, imported from the Team Database

items.label: Owned by
items.text: Store General Settings, Epic A (Edit Store Details → Team Branding & Sport); Step 1 — Basics, Epic D

items.label: On Home
items.text: Rendered, editable via the existing component

items.label: Scope
items.text: Store-level, buttons and accents only

items.label: Owned by
items.text: Store General Settings, Epic I

items.label: On Home
items.text: Rendered, editable via the Prolook color picker

items.label: Team artwork library — primary, wordmark, alternates, sport variants, each with a production-readiness state
Scope
items.text: Team-level, persists across seasons

items.label: Owned by
items.text: Product Catalog Management, Epic I

items.label: On Home
items.text: Linked, not reproduced

items.label: The third one is deliberately not embedded
items.text: The artwork library lives on the Team, not the store, and is read by both the Artwork Editor and the brand customizer. Rendering a Team-scoped library inside a store-scoped panel invites a rep to think they are editing this store's marks when they are editing every store that team ever has. Home links to it and says which scope it is.

items.label: Components are reused, not rebuilt
items.text: The Team Logo drop zone and Team Colors control are the Step 1 / Settings controls. The theme color uses the Prolook color picker — the owning spec is explicit that "no bespoke picker is built for this card," and that applies here too.

blocks.heading: Theme color behavior is inherited whole
items: The swatch shows its source — Team default or Custom — so the rep can see at a glance whether anything is overridden.
Reset to team color is available on a custom color and re-arms future re-derivation.

Home carries the owning spec's helper copy stating the color applies to buttons and accents only. That copy exists specifically so a rep does not report the unchanged page background as a bug, and Home — a surface reps will land on far more often than Settings — needs it more than Settings does, not less.

blocks.heading: Epic H — League structure directory (League stores only)
items: An at-a-glance list of divisions and teams, each routing into My Team(s). This is the panel most directly answering "how often I got stuck on my teams."

items.label: League stores only
items.text: Given an Individual Team (Single-Team Locker) store, then this panel does not render. That store is one team with no division tier and no grouping UI — the My Team tab drops straight into the roster, so a directory would list one row pointing at the tab's own landing view.
items: This is a conditional panel inside a permanent tab, the same shape as the conditional Catalog & Decoration section inside the permanent Settings tab. It does not make the Home tab conditional.

items.label: Read-only, and deliberately so
items.text: The panel lists structure; it does not edit it. The structure editor is already one shared component with two hosts and a standing rule that any change to it must be assessed against both — a third host is a real cost and a directory does not need one (Governing rule 1).

items.label: Contents
items.text: the same divisions · teams · players counts the My Team(s) stats header reports, then division rows with their teams nested beneath, then standalone teams listed separately — mirroring the tab's own arrangement of the canvas plus a standalone-teams list.

items: Each row carries its player count, and its pending Roster Bank capture count where any exist. Capture counts already surface on division cards, team cards, and the stats header; Home is one more read of the same figure, not a new one.

items.label: Clicking routes into My Team(s), scoped
items.text: A division opens that division; a team opens that team's detail. Given a team is targeted, then My Team(s) opens with the containing division auto-opened and breadcrumbs intact — the existing jump-in behavior. A row that dumps the rep on the canvas to find the team themselves reproduces the exact problem this panel exists to solve.

items.label: What this panel does not show
items.text: product thumbnail strips, division product-count pills, coverage tables, or the catalog drawer. Those are the workspace canvas surfaces in Roster Management Epic 6. Home is a directory, not a second canvas — and C-07 already carries the coverage gap into the attention list, which is where a gap belongs.

items.label: Team codes are not shown
items.text: They are backend routing keys, not rep-facing identifiers, and are surfaced in the workspace for reference and support rather than for navigation.

items.label: Divisions always render collapsed, at every league size
items.text: Each division row shows its name and its counts; clicking expands it to reveal its teams. The panel scrolls within a bounded height so it can never push the attention list off-screen.

items.label: There is deliberately no size threshold
items.text: A rule like "expand when under four divisions" was considered and rejected: it gives the rep a different page shape depending on their store, adds a number that can be wrong, and the collapsed row already carries the at-a-glance content the panel exists for. Predictability is worth more here than saving one click on a small league.

items.label: Expansion is per session, not persisted
items.text: Home holds no state (Governing rule 1), so an expanded division does not survive a reload.

items: On Archived stores, rows render and route to the read-only surfaces.

blocks.heading: Card copy — the rule, and the terms it bans
items: Card copy is specified here, not in the Epic C catalogue. Three rules, in priority order:

items.label: 1. Name the consequence, then the action
items.text: The headline says what is or isn't happening to someone; the detail line and button say what the rep does about it.

items.label: 2. No internal state names
items.text: If a rep would not use the word out loud to another rep, it does not go on a card.

items.label: 3. Say who is affected
items.text: Customers, players, orders, or a named division — not "the system", not the passive voice.

items.label: C-12 keeps the word bundle but drops "Incomplete"
items.text: Bundle is rep-facing; Incomplete is a state name from Products Epic J. Verify whether reps see that state label on the Products tab — if they do, the card may use it; if it's internal, it stays off.

items.label: C-18, C-20, and C-23 deliberately reassure
items.text: All three are Informational conditions that a rep may have caused on purpose or cannot act on. Per Governing rule 3, Home reports and does not scold — "nothing needed from you" and "this is fine if it's intentional" are doing real work.

items.label: No card uses the word "blocked"
items.text: It names the block rather than the fix, which is precisely the C-03 defect.

blocks.heading: The tier is not displayed on the card — decided
items: The tier is not shown on the card. A prototype rendered a red BLOCKING eyebrow above C- 03; it was removed.

Tier is a spec-internal ordering property, and displaying it fails rule 2 above like any other internal term. If the headline names the consequence properly the eyebrow is redundant; if it doesn't, the eyebrow is compensating for weak copy. A red all-caps BLOCKING on something the rep may not have caused also sits badly against the never-scold rule. The rail colour carries severity for scanning, which is all it needs to do.

blocks.heading: Product vocabulary
items: Home is a high-traffic surface and, if it becomes the landing tab, the rep's first exposure to the product's vocabulary on every visit. Its copy is therefore bound to the current labels and must be re-checked whenever they change — the same constraint and for the same reason as the Setup Guide's card copy.

items.label: Bound terms as of September 3, 2026
items.text: Stock Vault (not Product Vault), Catalog Templates (not Product Packages), Customizer (not Brand Catalog), Other stores, My Team(s), Roster Bank, Pending Orders, Submit (not approve), Open (not Active), Closed (not Paused / On Hold), Draft, Archived, Point of Contact (not Primary, not Primary Contact).

items.label: Status vocabulary is the lifecycle spec's, without exception
items.text: The canonical states are Draft, Open, Closed, Archived. Home must not render "Active" — a state that survives only in the stale Launch & Status Controls page. The workspace header's chip should be corrected on the same pass (Appendix A, 10).

items.label: Cards name the consequence, not the internal state
items.text: "Customers can't order these yet" over "visibility is off".

items.label: Cards never scold
items.text: No "you forgot", no "overdue", no red on an Informational condition. The rep is operating a store, not failing a checklist — the same tonal constraint the Setup Guide rewrite was driven by.

items.label: No completion, readiness, or score language anywhere on the page
items.text: Not in the attention list, not in the resume trail, not in the summary rail. This is a hard prohibition, inherited from the Setup Guide's "not a checklist" rule and extended here because Home is far more tempting to gamify.
